name: Marianus Scholasticus
bio: Marianus Scholasticus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no firm date for the poet. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, the sixth-century anthology.
This archive carries the 5 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 626, 627, 657, 668, 669).

poems.title: Book IX, 626: On another Bath called Love
poems.author: Marianus Scholasticus
poems.text: Love once bathed his mother Cypris in this bath, himself warming its lovely water with his torch. Ah, what a scent of spring had the sweat that ran from her ambrosial body mixing with the clear, white water! Henceforth from it ever bubbles a vapour smelling of roses, as if golden Cypris were still bathing.

poems.title: Book IX, 627
poems.author: Marianus Scholasticus
poems.text: Here under the plane-trees tired Love lay softly sleeping, having entrusted his torch to the Nymphs. Said the Nymphs among themselves: “Why not do it at once? Would that together with this we could put out the fire in men’s hearts.” But it was the torch that set fire to the water, and henceforth the Love-Nymphs pour forth here hot water for men to bathe in.

poems.title: Book IX, 657: On the Palace called Sophianae
poems.author: Marianus Scholasticus
poems.text: Where the land is cut in two by the winding channel whose shores open the way to the sea, our divine emperor erected this palace for his most illustrious consort Sophia. O, far-ruling Rome,’ thou lookest from Europe on a prospect in Asia the beauty of which is worthy of thee.

poems.title: Book IX, 668: On a Suburban Park in Amasia called Eros
poems.author: Marianus Scholasticus
poems.text: Verily it is lovely, the grove of Eros, where these beautiful trees are stirred by the gentle breath of Zephyr, where the dewy meadow is bright with flowers, sending up a wealthy show of purple-fringed cups, while the roses of three fountains in a line one after the other spout forth the streams of the sweet Naiad. Here Iris, the ancient river, swims past the woods, resort of the soft-haired Hamadryads, eee eee and in the fruitful vineyard the fat berries of the olive-trees flourish everywhere above the great clusters of raisins set out to dry. Around sing the nightingales, and the cicada hymns an answering harmony. Do not, stranger, pass by my open gate, but enter the house and partake of my simple hospitality.

poems.title: Book IX, 669: On the Same
poems.author: Marianus Scholasticus
poems.text: Come here for a little, traveller, and reclining in the greenwood shade rest thy limbs from thy long and toilsome journey. Here amongst the plane-trees the fresh streams of water running at its will leap forth beautifully from many-mouthed fountains. Here in spring the soft violets mixed with roses empurple the ground. Look how, engarlanding the fresh meadow, the luxuriant ivy twines its flowing hair. The river runs between its foliaged banks, grazing the base of the self-sown grove. Such is Eros. What other name would be appropriate for a place replete in every way with charm and loveliness ?
